item.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
item.author: Editorial
item.content:encoded: It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remainsAndy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage admits that Brexit was botched. But he wants greater divergence from, rather than increased closeness to, Europe. Both rightwing parties face a dilemma: how to oppose the better relationship when even Mr Farage acknowledges its benefits?Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? item.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalismIt’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.Continue reading...

item.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
item.author: Henrietta Moore
item.content:encoded: It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workersAI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programmeContinue reading...

item.title: Outages, spies, and trillion-dollar IPOs: is this our AI future? – Stateside with Kai and Carter
item.author: Hosted by Kai Wright , produced by Suzanne Gaber and Tiara Chiaramonte , engineered by Ivan Kuraev , executive producer Rachel Humphreys
item.content:encoded: It has been a wild few weeks in the world of tech. First, Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, forced an unimaginable leadership change at Nvidia – arguably the most consequential company in AI development. Then, chaos erupted as a rolling set of IT outages disrupted flights, banking, tech companies and the federal government. And now, Anthropic is blowing minds with a trillion-dollar IPO – one of the largest in stock market history. The Atlantic’s tech writer Charlie Warzel tells Kai Wright that these events are linked: they’re all examples of the ways in which we shoulder unprecedented risk today, in order to bet on AI’s future reward. It’s a convoluted logic that keeps the AI race speeding forward, no matter how many warning signs it blows past. Charlie Warzel is also host of the Atlantic’s podcast Galaxy Brain.Continue reading...

item.content:encoded: Julia Garner and Anthony Boyle play the FTX founders behind ‘the greatest fraud ever committed’ in the US. It’s a mind-boggling story – just make sure you don’t miss a single momentWhat happens when you put really stupid clever people in charge of the world? Not as presidents (they currently trend mostly towards the merely stupid) or prime ministers (generally neither really stupid nor really clever), but in charge of the real world, which is to say the online world, the one that really governs us? We are watching that play out day by day, but if you have enough slack left in your dread-system, a cortisol spike yet to execute, why not add a warning from history to your consumption of horrors?Welcome to The Altruists, a breakneck breakdown of the brief career of Sam Bankman-Fried (played by Anthony Boyle) who, with his on-off girlfriend Caroline Ellison (played by Julia Garner), set up the cryptocurrency exchange FTX with the belief that it would revolutionise finance and – as the increasingly absurd/dishonest/knowingly satirical Silicon Valley mantra has it – make the world a better place. A very few years later, FTX – worth $36bn (£27bn) at its peak – collapsed and in 2023 the pair were convicted of various charges deriving from what the trial judge called “the greatest financial fraud ever perpetrated in this country”. Ellison was sentenced to two years in prison after testifying against Bankman-Fried. Bankman-Fried is serving 25 years and was ordered to forfeit $11bn (£8.3bn). He says he is innocent and is applying to the supreme court to review his conviction.Continue reading...

item.title: Grade I interiors, gold bars, cost fears: Bank of England faces headache over £160m revamp
item.author: Phillip Inman
item.content:encoded: UK central bank will want to avoid echoes of expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that led to Trump clashAndrew Bailey may spend his days closely watching developments in the strait of Hormuz or US stock markets for signs of shocks to the global economy – but the Bank of England’s governor has a £160m problem brewing much closer to home.A secretive major revamp of the Bank’s historic headquarters in the heart of London’s Square Mile presents a huge test of Bailey’s project management skills. The central bank, with its reputation staked on carefully counting the nation’s pennies, will be keen to avoid delays, budget-busting or any echoes of the expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that left his former peer Jerome Powell awkwardly clashing with Donald Trump on camera.Continue reading...

item.title: Private renters in England: have you struggled to get your deposit back?
item.author: Guardian community team
item.content:encoded: We would like to hear from private tenants about their experiences of the rental deposit system in EnglandIn May 2026, the government overhauled private renting by abolishing no-fault evictions and shifting private tenancies to rolling contracts. However, deposit protection remains an issue for many private renters.The government has promised and begun consulting on reforms, including scrapping insured deposit schemes, but has yet to confirm when this will happen. Landlords and letting agents are currently permitted to hold tenant deposits in their own bank accounts and this creates a “power imbalance”, housing and planning minister Matthew Pennycook has said.Continue reading...

item.title: Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers
item.author: Hilary Osborne Consumer and money editor
item.content:encoded: It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the forecast rise next yearThe energy price cap in Great Britain looks likely to go up by 26% in January. But your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving.Providers are offering fixed tariffs that work out up to £407 below the estimated price cap, according to price comparison website uSwitch. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use.Continue reading...

The department said workers doing routine digging in an area that had not been worked on for some time hit a deposit of gases. Officials initially said a pipe had been struck.
